source.title: Current Unsolved Problems in Planetary Nebulae Research

accepted.question_text: What definition of a planetary nebula is precise enough to distinguish a true planetary nebula from observational mimics such as emission-line galaxies, reflection nebulae, H II regions, Wolf-Rayet nebulae, novae, supernova remnants, young stellar objects, and symbiotic stars, while still requiring both an ionized circumstellar shell and the correct evolutionary connection to an asymptotic giant branch progenitor and its hot post-AGB or pre-white-dwarf central star?

evidence.quote: The question of "what is a planetary nebula" is not as straightforward as one might think.
Most fundamentally, we need a clear definition of the planetary nebula phenomenon so that our studies are not confused with objects in other stages of stellar evolution.

accepted.question_text: What are the true intrinsic three-dimensional structures of planetary nebulae, and how can observers reliably recover those structures from two-dimensional images and kinematic data when projection effects can make nebulae with similar 3D morphologies appear very different on the sky and can hide multipolar structure until deeper or infrared observations are obtained?

evidence.quote: These include the true 3D morphological structure of the nebulae, origin of multipolar nebulae, the dust and molecular distribution relative to the optical nebulosity, large-scale structures outside of the main nebulae, the relevance of binarity to planetary nebulae evolution, and a precise definition of the planetary nebula phenomenon.
Kinematic mapping of both the ionized and neutral components would allow us to develop a comprehensive true 3D model of planetary nebulae.

accepted.question_text: What physical process first creates the asymmetries that later develop into bipolar, multipolar, or point-symmetric planetary nebula morphologies, and at what evolutionary stage do those asymmetries first appear: during the asymptotic giant branch wind, during the proto-planetary-nebula phase, or only after the fast post-AGB wind turns on?

evidence.quote: What is the origin of such asymmetries and when did they first develop?

Imaging with the HST showed that they already possess bipolar and, in some cases, multipolar shapes, which was interpreted as indicating that much of the shaping happened early in the proto-planetary nebulae phase or even in the late-AGB phase [60–63].

accepted.question_text: What mechanism creates the highly collimated fast outflows seen in some planetary nebulae, including rotating jets and multiple bipolar lobes at different orientations, when the ordinary central-star fast wind is largely spherical and simple binary-merger scenarios do not explain recurrent or differently oriented ejection events?

evidence.quote: The mechanisms responsible for the creation of these collimated outflows are not known.

The existence of multipolar nebulae is probably the result of collimated fast outflows penetrating the pre-existing AGB circumstellar envelope, but the mechanism responsible for producing such outflows is unclear.

accepted.question_text: If the concentric arcs and rings seen around some planetary nebulae and proto-planetary nebulae are signatures of episodic outflows, what physical process sets the recurrence timescale of those episodes, and what causes successive outflows or lobes to change direction between primary and secondary bipolar axes?

evidence.quote: If the 2D concentric rings are the result of episodic outflows, what determines the period of the episodes?
The presence of secondary bipolar lobes along directions different from the primary lobes suggests that episodic outflows could also change directions.

accepted.question_text: Do the cometary globules and dense clumps seen in planetary nebulae form during the planetary-nebula phase itself, perhaps through instabilities at an ionization front, or are they already present as clumps in the asymptotic giant branch wind and able to survive the transition into the planetary-nebula phase to become the observed knots?

evidence.quote: The origin of globules remains under discussion.

Whether these clumps can survive through the transition to the planetary nebulae phase to be responsible for the knots seen in planetary nebulae is unclear, as they are not in pressure equilibrium with the surrounding wind.

accepted.question_text: What is the origin of the compact disks or torus-like structures found around some planetary-nebula central stars and in bipolar systems, and how, if at all, do those disks or accretion structures generate or collimate the directional outflows that shape narrow-waist bipolar or multipolar nebulae?

evidence.quote: The origin of these disks is not known.
Currently, the physical origin of the directional outflows and the collimating mechanisms are unknown.
However, the origin of such disks is uncertain.

accepted.question_text: What are the full three-dimensional distributions of the molecular gas, dust, and other neutral material in planetary nebulae relative to the ionized optical nebula, and what role does that neutral component play in confining optical lobes, setting the true mass distribution, and collimating or shaping bipolar outflows?

evidence.quote: An accurate determination of the distribution of the neutral component of planetary nebulae is essential in our understanding of the actual mass distribution of planetary nebulae.
While the ionized component can be easily imaged, the distributions of molecular gas and dust in planetary nebulae are yet to be well determined.
A complete mapping of the neutral component is crucial in understanding the role of the neutral component in collimating and confining outflows.

accepted.question_text: How can complex organic compounds form in the low-density circumstellar environments of planetary nebulae during or after post-asymptotic-giant-branch evolution, given that the observed unidentified infrared emission bands imply substantial chemical synthesis under conditions that are not yet physically understood?

evidence.quote: How such complex organic compounds can be formed in the low-density circumstellar environment remains a major unsolved problem in modern astrochemistry [125].

accepted.question_text: What physical mechanisms produce the unexpectedly large outer structures and giant bipolar lobes seen around some planetary nebulae, including parsec-scale or degree-scale outflows with hypersonic expansion velocities, and how frequently do the eruptive or post-common-envelope events capable of launching such structures actually occur?

evidence.quote: The existence of large-scale structures in planetary nebulae is unexpected and the physical mechanisms responsible for the large dimensions and hypersonic expansion velocities are not known.
The frequency of occurrence of such events is uncertain.

accepted.question_text: Where are the binary companions that are often invoked as the drivers of proto-planetary-nebula shaping, and if they remain undetected, are they predominantly very low-mass companions such as stars below 0.2 solar masses, brown dwarfs, or planets, or instead companions on orbital periods longer than about 30 years?

evidence.quote: Thus there is no direct evidence of a close binary companion in any of the proto-planetary nebulae.

So, we seem to be left with the following unanswered questions: Where are the binary companions thought to be the drivers of the shaping of the nebulae in proto-planetary nebulae? Are they low-mass (<0.2 Mʘ ) stars or even brown dwarfs or planets, or do they have long (>30 yr) periods?

accepted.question_text: What objects are the actual progenitors of planetary nebulae with close binary central stars, if the currently identified proto-planetary nebulae do not appear to evolve into that population, and does planetary-nebula formation proceed through two distinct channels: gradual post-AGB evolution and common-envelope evolution?

evidence.quote: Where are the progenitors of the close binary central stars of planetary nebulae? They do not appear to be the identified proto-planetary nebulae.
Are there two different ways, gradual post-AGB evolution and common-envelope evolution, for planetary nebulae to form from AGB stars?

accepted.question_text: How do hierarchical triple stellar systems evolve before and during the asymptotic giant branch and planetary-nebula phases, and what morphological or dynamical effects do such triples produce on the resulting nebular outflows once inner-binary hardening, mergers, and possible loss or survival of the outer component are taken into account?

evidence.quote: There are many uncertainties about how hierarchical triples evolve, and in what state they reach the AGB and planetary nebulae phase [178].

accepted.question_text: What is the physical origin of the planetary-nebula abundance discrepancy in which recombination lines yield much higher abundances than forbidden lines, where in the nebula is the hypothesized cool hydrogen-poor component located, and by what mechanism could close-binary or common-envelope evolution generate the extreme abundance discrepancy factors observed in some systems?

evidence.quote: As the forbidden lines are temperature-sensitive, the difference is commonly attributed to a cool, hydrogen-poor component of the nebula [184], but the nature and location of this component is unclear.
But it is unclear how common-envelope evolution could cause the ADF anomaly.

accepted.question_text: Why does the bright-end cutoff of the planetary-nebula luminosity function appear nearly invariant across extragalactic stellar populations of very different ages when stellar-evolution models still struggle to reproduce that invariance completely, especially in old populations where star formation ceased more than about 5 Gyr ago?

evidence.quote: Models of stellar evolution have had difficulty explaining this invariance: they predict more planetary nebulae at luminosities above the cut-off, and a lower cut-off in older systems.
The faster evolution shown by the new post-AGB stellar evolution models [170] has resolved part of the discrepancies [186] but not all [187].
